title: This world and no other
theme: The hereafter never dawns on the heedless, dazed by wealth; thinking ‘this world, no other’, he falls into Death’s power again and again.

words.meaning: what concerns the passing-on; the means to the next world

words.role: the one to whom it does not appear
subject of the first quoted clause (‘this world [exists]’)
verb of the second quoted clause

sandhi.type: final m before a consonant; aḥ before a voiced consonant; savarṇa-dīrgha
sandhi.rule: ayam before l: P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः). lokaḥ before n: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). na + asti: a + a give ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: The visarga becomes y, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य); the hiatus stays.

sandhi.type: r before a voiced consonant; final m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: punar ends in r, which is kept before the voiced v (it becomes visarga only before a pause or a voiceless sound, P. 8.3.15 (खरवसानयोर्विसर्जनीयः)). vaśam keeps its m before ā.

morphology.note: A derivative (with vṛddhi of the first syllable) of samparāya ‘the passing-on, the hereafter’: ‘what concerns the hereafter’. Śaṅkara explains both: «सम्परेयत इति सम्परायः परलोकः», and the derivative as the scriptural means of reaching it.
Present participle of pra-mad, fourth class (the stem vowel lengthened: mādya-): ‘being careless, distracted’.
mānin, an agent noun of man ‘think’: one who habitually thinks so. It can also mean ‘proud, conceited’, which is how Raṅgarāmānuja takes it: «‘मानी’ इत्यस्य दुर्मानीत्यर्थः».

translation.literal: ‘The hereafter does not shine upon the child, heedless, deluded by the delusion of wealth. “This [is the] world; there is no other”: thinking so, he comes again and again into my power.’
translation.readable: ‘What lies beyond never dawns on the childish, careless and dazed by wealth. “This world is all there is,” he thinks, “there is no other” — and so he falls into my hands again and again.’

anvaya: प्रमाद्यन्तम् वित्तमोहेन मूढम् बालम् साम्परायः न प्रतिभाति । अयम् लोकः [अस्ति], परः न अस्ति इति मानी पुनः पुनः मे वशम् आपद्यते ।
syntax: Two sentences. In the first, sāmparāyaḥ is the subject of na pratibhāti, and the accusative bālam, with two participles and an instrumental of cause, names the person to whom it does not appear. In the second, a quoted thought closed by iti — ‘this [is the] world; there is no other’ — is held by mānī, the subject of āpadyate; me, ‘my’, is Death’s.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara takes it as the scriptural means of reaching the next world, derived from samparāya, the next world itself: «सम्परेयत इति सम्परायः परलोकः, तत्प्राप्तिप्रयोजनः साधनविशेषः शास्त्रीयः साम्परायः». Raṅgarāmānuja: the activity that secures the next world, «परलोकसाधनव्यापारः». At 1.1.29 the same word named the passing-on itself.

ambiguities.topic: ‘This world; there is no other’ — or ‘neither this nor the other’
ambiguities.note: Both commentators read: only this world exists, there is no other. Raṅgarāmānuja reports that on the sūtra BS 3.1.13 the verse was read «अयं लोको नास्ति पर उत मानी» and explained as denying both worlds, «अयं च लोकः परश्च लोको नास्तीत्यर्थो वर्णितः»; he adds that the reading is not accepted by the learned, «शिष्टपरिग्रहाभावात्».

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: The halves count 22 and 23. The third pāda, ayaṃ loko nāsti para iti mānī, has 12, with the hiatus para iti counted as written; the other pādas have 11.

beginner: Having described those who think they are wise, Death describes where their thinking leads. To a childish person, careless and dazzled by money, the question of what lies beyond death never even comes up. Such a person decides that this world is all there is and that there is nothing after it. Death then says, quietly, that this person comes into his power again and again. In the Upaniṣad’s picture, refusing to think about death does not protect anyone from it; it only means meeting it over and over, in birth after birth, without ever understanding it. The verse is the opposite of Naciketas, a boy who walked into Death’s house to ask exactly the question that others avoid.
analogy: Like a student who decides there will be no examination and so never studies, and keeps sitting the same examination again.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the hereafter does not occur to the heedless, the person dazed by wealth, who thinks ‘this world is all; there is no other’; and that such a person comes into Death’s power again and again.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: being born again and again and falling under the control of Death: «पुनः पुनः जनित्वा वशम् अधीनताम् आपद्यते मे मृत्योर्मम», that is, riding a chain of sorrows marked by birth and death, «जननमरणादिलक्षणदुःखप्रबन्धारूढ एव भवतीत्यर्थः». Raṅgarāmānuja: he becomes the object of the torments Death inflicts, «मत्क्रियमाणयातना विषयो भवति इत्यर्थः».

commentary.q: How is the verse used elsewhere?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Śaṅkara quotes it in full in his Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya on 3.1.13, the sūtra on the fate of evildoers, as a scripture in the words of Yama himself that shows them falling under his control: «अनिष्टादिकारिणां यमवश्यतां दर्शयति».

commentary.q: What is the force of mānī?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: An agent noun from man ‘think’: ‘one who [habitually] thinks so’ — Śaṅkara: «इत्येवं मननशीलः मानी». Since mānin also means ‘proud’, Raṅgarāmānuja reads ‘wrongly proud’: «दुर्मानी».

advaita.text: The careless person sees only this visible world, «स्त्र्यन्नपानादिविशिष्टः», denies the unseen one, and so remains in the round of birth and death under Death’s control.

visistadvaita.text: Thinking that only this world exists and the other does not, «अयमेव लोकोऽस्ति; परलोको नास्तीति मन्यमानः», he becomes subject to the torments Death inflicts.

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara stresses repeated birth and death; Raṅgarāmānuja the torments in Yama’s realm, the reading the Brahmasūtra (3.1.13) also gives. Madhva comments on the passage 1.2.4–8 only at 1.2.8.

parallels.note: ‘But the others, having experienced [their deserts] in Saṃyamana, ascend and descend, for their course is seen [in scripture].’ Śaṅkara’s bhāṣya on this sūtra cites this verse as the scripture that shows it.

parallels.quote: न साम्परायः प्रतिभाति बालं प्रमाद्यन्तं वित्तमोहेन मूढम्
parallels.note: Śaṅkara’s Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya quotes the whole verse, with the reference (क. उ. १ । २ । ६), as ‘a scripture in the form of Yama’s words’.
‘The utterly deluded know no other good’: the Muṇḍaka’s ritualists, like the Kaṭha’s careless man, see nothing beyond what they already have, and return to this world or a lower one.

contemporary.text: It is possible to live for decades without once asking seriously what a life is for or what death means, especially when there is money to spend and much to do. The verse does not threaten such a person with punishment so much as describe a pattern: the question avoided keeps returning, at every loss and every illness, until it is faced. This is a reflection, not part of the commentaries.

reflect.beginner: When did the question of death last come to your mind, and what did you do with it?
reflect.deeper: Is ‘this world is all there is’ a conclusion people reach, or a habit of not looking?
reflect.practice: Spend five quiet minutes with the question Naciketas asked, without trying to answer it.

flags.note: Coming into Death’s power: repeated birth and death (Śaṅkara) or the torments of Yama’s realm (Raṅgarāmānuja, with BS 3.1.13).
